lead: Macaulay's method writes one bending moment equation for the whole beam, using bracket terms that switch on only after the section passes a load. One expression means one pair of integration constants and no matching of segments. It is the standard exam route for a simply supported or cantilever beam carrying several loads, and the same brackets sit inside most beam-analysis software. This chapter shows the brackets, the integration rule and the support conditions that finish the job.
prereq: You need 5.1 for EI y″ = M, 5.2 for the integrate-twice routine, and the SFD/BMD work of Unit 3 for the reactions.

blocks.text: In the double integration method you split the beam into segments between loads. Each segment needs its own M(x), its own two constants, and matching conditions at every junction. Three loads give four sets of algebra and three chances to slip.
Macaulay's method keeps one expression from the left end to the right end. The trick is a bracket that stays asleep until the section passes the load.
⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = 0 when x < a;  ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = (x − a)ⁿ when x ≥ a
blocks.where: x is the distance from the left end to the section, in m; a is the distance from the left end to the load, in m; n is 0, 1 or 2 depending on the load type; the angle brackets are Macaulay's brackets.

blocks.text: Because the term is exactly zero up to a, adding it to M(x) changes nothing to the left of the load and adds the load's full contribution to the right. The single M(x) is then correct at every section.
Some syllabi call these Macaulay's brackets; others call the whole idea the singularity function method.

head: Load on the beam
Term added to M(x)
rows: Downward point load W at x = a
Applied moment M₀ at x = a
UDL w starting at x = a and running right
UDL w from x = a to x = b (it stops at b)

blocks.text: The signs above suit sagging positive with downward loads. W is in kN, w in kN/m, M₀ in kN·m, a and b in m.

items: Point load: its moment about the section is W times the lever arm (x − a), and it hogs, so the term is negative.
Applied moment: a concentrated couple has no lever arm, so it enters with power zero. ⟨x − a⟩⁰ is 1 after a and 0 before.
UDL starting at a: the load w(x − a) acts at its centroid (x − a)/2 from the section, giving w(x − a)²/2.
UDL that ends: a UDL from a to b is a UDL starting at a plus an upward UDL of the same w starting at b. Each start needs its own bracket, which is how you switch a load off.
Loads left of the origin never need a bracket. Always put the origin at the left end and reuse the same sign convention.
Draw the free body diagram and get both reactions from ΣF and ΣM (Unit 3).
Write EI d²y/dx² = M(x) with every load as a bracket term.
Integrate once for slope: each ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ becomes ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1). Add C₁.
Integrate again for deflection and add C₁x + C₂. No bracket gets its own constant, because M(x) is a single function.
Put y = 0 at each support: x = 0 gives C₂ for a beam resting at the left end, and x = L gives C₁. A cantilever fixed at x = 0 uses y = 0 and y′ = 0 instead.
Substitute the x where deflection is wanted. If x < a, write 0 for that bracket — never a negative number.

blocks.text: One power is special. ⟨x − a⟩⁰ integrates to ⟨x − a⟩¹, not to x, because the bracket stays zero until x reaches a.

The method needs reactions that statics alone can give. In a propped cantilever or a fixed beam the reactions are themselves unknown, so the brackets are combined with an extra compatibility equation — see 5.8. For a quick deflection check on a simple load case, 5.6 is faster.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a point load of 10 kN at 2 m from the left end and a UDL of 4 kN/m over the whole span. EI = 6000 kN·m². Use Macaulay's method to find the deflection under the point load.
steps: Reactions. Total UDL = 4 × 6 = 24 kN, acting at midspan, 3 m from the left end. Taking moments about the left support A: R_B × 6 = 10 × 2 + 24 × 3 = 20 + 72 = 92 kN·m, so R_B = 15.333 kN and R_A = 10 + 24 − 15.333 = 18.667 kN.
Moment expression. Origin at A, sagging positive: M(x) = 18.667x − 10⟨x − 2⟩ − (4/2)x² = 18.667x − 10⟨x − 2⟩ − 2x², in kN·m, with x in m.
First integration: EI y′ = 9.333x² − 5⟨x − 2⟩² − 0.6667x³ + C₁, in kN·m².
Second integration: EI y = 3.111x³ − 1.667⟨x − 2⟩³ − 0.1667x⁴ + C₁x + C₂, in kN·m³.
Support at x = 0. Every x term and every bracket is zero there, so C₂ = 0.
Deflection at x = 2, under the point load. The bracket ⟨x − 2⟩ is zero here: EI y = 3.111 × 8 − 0 − 0.1667 × 16 + (−58.222) × 2 = 24.889 − 2.667 − 116.444 = −94.222 kN·m³.
y = −94.222/6000 = −0.0157037 m = −15.70 mm. With y positive upward, the negative sign means the beam moves down.
examples.answer: The deflection under the point load is 15.70 mm downward, that is y = −15.70 mm. Check values: R_A = 18.667 kN, C₁ = −58.222 kN·m².

traps: Putting a negative number into a bracket instead of writing zero. ⟨x − 4⟩³ at x = 1 is 0, not −27.
Adding a fresh constant after integrating each bracket. The whole EI y needs only C₁ and C₂.
Forgetting to switch off a UDL that ends partway, so the load keeps acting to the right end and the reactions no longer balance.
Losing the sign convention: EI y″ = M is used with y positive upward, so a sagging beam gives a negative y at midspan.
Trying Macaulay's method on a propped cantilever without writing the compatibility equation first — the reactions cannot be found from statics alone.

quiz.q: Define ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ in words and as a formula.
quiz.a: It is zero when x < a and equals (x − a)ⁿ when x ≥ a. It is called a Macaulay bracket or singularity function.

quiz.q: What power of bracket represents a concentrated applied moment, and what does it integrate to?
quiz.a: Power zero. It integrates to ⟨x − a⟩¹, not to x.

quiz.q: Why does a single bracketed moment expression stay correct at every section instead of needing one equation per segment?
quiz.a: Each bracket is exactly zero before its load position, so the expression matches the true moment there; after that position the bracket adds the load's full contribution. Hence one function covers all segments.

quiz.q: Why is there no new integration constant for each bracket term?
quiz.a: M(x) is integrated as a single function of x. Two integrations give exactly two arbitrary constants, C₁ and C₂, whichever brackets appear in the expression.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 8 m has a 20 kN point load at 3 m from the left end and a 5 kN/m UDL over the whole span. Find the reactions and write M(x) with brackets.
For the beam above with EI = 4000 kN·m², write EI y after two integrations, keeping the constants general.
A student applies Macaulay's method to a beam fixed at both ends and gets nonsense. What is missing?
quiz.a: Both end moments are unknown, so the beam is statically indeterminate and the reactions cannot come from statics alone. An extra compatibility condition on deflection or slope at a support must be added, as in 5.8, before one bracketed M(x) can be written.

beyond: Not for the exam. Macaulay brackets are the same idea as the singularity functions used in structural analysis software: a beam is stored as a list of loads with positions, and the moment is built by summing bracket terms, so the program never splits the beam into segments. In mathematics the same objects build step functions and the Dirac delta, the derivative of ⟨x − a⟩⁰. Finite element codes go further and use shape functions instead. Search 'singularity functions beam deflection' or 'Macaulay brackets in structural analysis code' to go deeper.
